analysis.one_liner: Caps U.S. drug prices within 6% of what five other wealthy countries charge for the same drugs.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had no cosponsors, was referred to two House committees and never received a hearing or a vote before the 107th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have ordered the President to set rules ensuring no drug sold to American consumers costs more than 6% above the average retail price charged for that same drug in the five largest industrialized free-market countries other than the United States. It gave federal investigators subpoena power to examine drugmakers' pricing records, authorized court injunctions, civil penalties of up to twice the unjust enrichment, criminal fines up to 200% of the sale amount, and let consumers and class-action plaintiffs sue violators for damages plus attorneys' fees. The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Judiciary committees in April 2001, sent to subcommittees, and never advanced any further.
analysis.who_benefits: American consumers who buy prescription drugs, especially those paying out of pocket for medications priced far above what the same drugs cost in countries like Canada, France, Germany, Japan, and the United Kingdom. The bill's civil liability provisions, including class actions with attorneys' fees, would give overcharged consumers a way to recover.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Prescription drug buyers in the U.S.

how_it_helps.text: Directs the President to issue orders and regulations ensuring no pharmaceutical product is sold to U.S. consumers at a price more than 6% above the average retail price in the five most industrialized free-market countries other than the United States.
Grants federal officers subpoena power to examine drugmakers' books and records and compel testimony to enforce the pricing limits, with court-backed penalties for refusal.
Authorizes federal injunctions, restitution of illegally collected money, civil penalties of up to 200% of unjust enrichment, and criminal fines of up to 200% of each violating sale.
Creates a private right of action letting overcharged consumers recover actual damages, punitive damages, and attorneys' fees, including through class actions.

analysis.who_pays: Pharmaceutical manufacturers would bear the cost, either by lowering U.S. prices to the international benchmark or facing penalties. If companies responded by raising prices in the other five countries to soften the comparison, foreign consumers and governments could pay more.

drawbacks.text: The bill hands the President broad discretion to define covered products and the foreign reference prices by regulation, an unusual delegation of price-setting power to the executive branch that critics of price controls would view as legally and institutionally problematic.

A cap tied to foreign prices could reduce pharmaceutical revenues, and the bill's own findings acknowledge producers must be 'appropriately compensated'; supporters of drug-industry pricing argue lower expected returns could slow investment in new medicines.

Enforcement depends on knowing retail prices in five other countries, giving drugmakers an incentive to raise prices abroad, which could import foreign price pressure rather than simply lowering U.S. prices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is straightforward: Americans pay roughly the same for patented drugs as people in comparable countries, and the bill backs the cap with real enforcement and consumer lawsuits. The serious cost is design quality: this is a one-page grant of sweeping price-setting discretion to the President, introduced without cosponsors, and it does not address how drugmakers might game the foreign-price benchmark or what happens to research incentives. It is a strong statement of principle with a blunt instrument attached.

outcome.mechanism: It died quietly in committee: referred to two House committees, sent to subcommittees, and never taken up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Major Owens introduced the Pharmaceutical Products Price Equity Act on April 24, 2001.
The bill was referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce and, in addition, to the Committee on the Judiciary.
On May 4, 2001 it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health, and on September 28, 2001 to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Courts, the Internet, and Intellectual Property.
No further action was taken before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003, and the bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmaceutical manufacturers, who kept charging U.S. consumers prices above those in other wealthy countries with no risk of the cap or its penalties taking effect.

sides.party_line_note: The record shows a single Democratic sponsor and no Republican or Democratic cosponsors; the bill was referred to committees run by Republicans and never taken up.

industries.note: The bill would cap U.S. retail prices at roughly parity with five foreign markets, backed by criminal fines, civil penalties, restitution, and consumer class actions. Because Americans currently pay some of the world's highest drug prices, the industry's financial interest in this bill ran directly against the interests of U.S. drug buyers.
Ordinary drug buyers, especially those paying out of pocket, would pay no more than about 6% above the benchmark foreign price, and could sue for damages if overcharged.
